activitySchema.heading: Read three line choices
activitySchema.instruction: Label A, B and C. Look at the marks, then match each place to its line choice.

items.label: A
items.feedback: A is one long curve. The point stays on the page along the curved route.

items.label: B
items.feedback: B has gaps. The point lifts on purpose between parts of the line.

items.label: C
items.feedback: C is a group of short strokes. Each stroke has its own start and end.

activitySchema.discussion: Choose one line to try with your own tool. Point to a place where your hand action changes the mark. Your result need not copy this model.

activitySchema.heading: Choose what changes tone
activitySchema.instruction: Sort each action. Does it change light and dark, or does it change something else?

items.label: Leave a patch of paper white.
items.feedback: White paper can keep a light area in the drawing.

items.label: Use a sheet that is twice as wide.
items.feedback: This changes the size of the sheet. It does not itself make a mark lighter or darker.

items.label: Add a gentle pencil layer over a patch.
items.feedback: A further pencil layer can darken the patch. Check what your own tool does.

items.label: Turn the paper so your arm has room.
items.feedback: This changes your reach. It can help you work, but is not itself a tone change.

activitySchema.discussion: Try a pale patch and a dark patch. Point to what you did to make each one. If they look alike, say so and check the action you used.

activitySchema.heading: Predict, then test the fold
activitySchema.instruction: Predict before the adult tests a paper tent. Choose a model answer, then check the real paper too.

items.label: The same tent is opened wider at its base. The two panels stay the same length. What happens to its top?
items.feedback: In this simple tent model, a wider base brings the top lower. Watch the adult open the same fold, then compare what you see.

options.label: It gets lower.
It gets higher.

items.label: The tent leans. What can we claim before trying a change?
items.feedback: We have a prediction to test. Try a small change in the fold or base. Use what the paper really does to decide what helped.

options.label: More tape will always fix it.
We need to test a change to its support.

activitySchema.discussion: Make your own fold. Test one change at a time. Keep a note of what you saw, even if the real result differs from your first idea.
activitySchema.staffNote: Use the same rectangular paper and crease for the first demonstration. The model predicts height, not guaranteed stability. A rigid diagram or an adult-held form can support access, but must not be recorded as a free-standing pupil form.

activitySchema.heading: Find the fault before adding tape
activitySchema.instruction: Spot the error in each claim. Choose a useful check. Then point to the place you would inspect on the adult model.

items.label: “The tab stayed attached, but the form tipped. The join must have failed.”
items.feedback: The tab stayed on. First check the base and how the whole form is supported.

options.label: Check the whole form and its base.
Add tape to every edge.

items.label: “The tape touches the tab only. It joins the tab to the form.”
items.feedback: A join must connect the two surfaces. Tape on just one does not bridge them.

options.label: Check that tape bridges both surfaces.
Press the untouched form harder.

items.label: “My first join came apart. I have learnt nothing.”
items.feedback: A failed join can show useful learning. Keep what really happened, then test a small change.

options.label: Hide the trial.
Keep the trial and name what came apart.

activitySchema.discussion: Test your own join. Show what stayed attached and what moved. Keep the result before changing it.

activitySchema.heading: Choose a question with a purpose
activitySchema.instruction: Everyone commits to a question before we compare. These classroom examples help us rehearse; they are not replies from the real artist or arts group.

items.label: You want to know how the artist made a thin curved mark. Which question points to that detail?
items.feedback: This question points to a mark in the work. The artist can explain the tool or action they used.

options.label: What tool made this thin curve?
What is your favourite lunch?

items.label: You want to know how an arts group helps people take part. Which question fits?
items.feedback: This asks about a role the group may have. Find out what the real group actually does.

options.label: How do you help someone try a new art tool?
Did you make every picture in the world?

items.label: No live or active session is confirmed yet. What should your preparation card say?
items.feedback: A preparation card helps you get ready. It does not prove that a real session took place.

options.label: The visit is complete.
The real experience is still to be arranged.

activitySchema.discussion: Now make your own question for the artist and one for the arts group. You may point, sign or ask through an adult. Keep both real experience needs open.
activitySchema.staffNote: These are illustrative questions, not a booked programme or substitute for Explore Part B. Keep artist exploration and arts organisation exploration distinct.

activitySchema.heading: Put a real experience record in order
activitySchema.instruction: Put these steps in order for a real artist session. Use each place once. If the session is not ready, this is practice.

items.label: Keep a true note of what you did and found out.
items.feedback: The record follows the action. Name the artist, session and what you actually explored.

items.label: Ask staff if the real session is ready. Check how you will take part.
items.feedback: Readiness comes first. Do not invent an experience while it is still being arranged.

items.label: Respond to what the artist shows or says.
items.feedback: Use the real exchange or activity to notice, try, ask or respond.

items.label: Join the real artist session in the agreed way.
items.feedback: Take part through the agreed route. An old film alone is preparation, not this session.

activitySchema.discussion: Tell the adult which step you can really do today. If it is practice time, keep that label and leave the real reply blank.

activitySchema.heading: Read an example arts space
activitySchema.instruction: This is a made-up arts room. Label A, B and C. Match each place to the job it could help people do.

items.label: A
items.feedback: The spaced works make it easier to see each piece. This example shows a display role.

items.label: B
items.feedback: The tools and work table can help people try making. An adult checks the actual tools and access needs.

items.label: C
items.feedback: The seats and speech marks show a place to ask and talk about the work.

activitySchema.discussion: Choose a job to ask the real arts group about. This picture is a made-up room. We still need to find out what the real group does.

activitySchema.heading: What can this record tell us?
activitySchema.instruction: Sort these made-up cases. Some help us get ready. Others keep what someone did in a real session.

items.label: A logo copied before an activity.
items.feedback: A logo can help identify a group. It does not show your active exploration.

items.label: A true note of a real artist session. It keeps what the pupil asked and how they responded.
items.feedback: This can record artist exploration when it accurately names the session and action.

items.label: Notes made only from an old film of a workshop.
items.feedback: The film may help you prepare. It does not itself show your live or active exploration.

items.label: A true note from a real arts group session. It keeps what the pupil did and found out.
items.feedback: This can record arts group exploration when its source and the real action are clear.

activitySchema.discussion: Find a detail in each of your real records. If one is missing, name what still needs to happen. These made-up cards are not your own work.

activitySchema.heading: Predict a print, then try it
activitySchema.instruction: Choose a prediction for the adult’s print test. Check the model reason, then test with the real tool on scrap paper.

items.label: The wet print tool slides sideways as it is lifted. What might happen to the edge?
items.feedback: A sideways move can drag the wet mark. Try a straight lift and a sideways move on scrap. Check the actual edges.

options.label: It may drag or blur.
It must become a sharper copy.

items.label: You want to compare rough and smooth paper. What would help you see the paper’s effect?
items.feedback: Keeping the tool and paint similar helps you compare the papers. Real print marks may still vary.

options.label: Use the same tool and similar paint for both.
Change the paper, tool and paint all at once.

items.label: A trial gave a mark you did not expect. What should you keep?
items.feedback: A surprising mark can guide a new choice. Keep the true result before deciding what to use.

options.label: Only a claim that it worked as planned.
The real test and what you noticed.

activitySchema.discussion: Make the two small tests. Point to a part that helped you choose. Keep your starting idea and the tests; the final artwork comes when you have made it.

activitySchema.heading: Keep the step before it is hidden
activitySchema.instruction: Order this four-step collage join. Use each position once. Then say why the loose layout is kept before glue is used.

items.label: Press the piece down, then check the dry edge.
items.feedback: Press gently. Once the join is ready, check for a loose corner.

items.label: Try the dry pieces and choose their overlap.
items.feedback: A loose trial lets you move shapes before they are fixed.

items.label: Put a thin coat of glue on the chosen piece.
items.feedback: Add glue after you have kept a record of the chosen loose layout.

items.label: Keep a sketch or image of the loose layout.
items.feedback: This saves a real making stage that the join will change.

activitySchema.discussion: Try the join on scraps. Ask before touching someone else’s work. A helper can steady the card; the layout choice stays yours.

activitySchema.heading: Find the missing before state
activitySchema.instruction: Spot the error in each plan. Choose a way to keep a true making step before it changes.

items.label: “I ringed the edge, then painted over the ring. The ring still records the old layout.”
items.feedback: A separate record remains when the area on the artwork is covered.

options.label: Keep a separate sketch or clear image before painting.
Paint over the rest so nothing can be checked.

items.label: “I will remember it, so no earlier work needs to be kept.”
items.feedback: Memory can help you talk. A kept trial or record lets someone see the making step too.

options.label: Keep a real trial or a clear record of the earlier state.
Write a different story after it is finished.

items.label: “The new strip must be better because it is new.”
items.feedback: A new piece is not automatically the right choice. You can keep the old layout for a reason.

options.label: Hide the earlier strip.
Compare the actual effect and keep your choice.

activitySchema.discussion: Try a light and dark piece beside the same print. Look at the edges. Save your trial before fixing the version you choose.

activitySchema.heading: Show what is ready to bank
activitySchema.instruction: Everyone commits before we compare. Choose what each example lets us claim. Use the actual work, not a promise.

items.label: A test strip shows two paint coats. What is it?
items.feedback: The strip shows a real trial. Keep it with the making record.

options.label: A process record.
The whole finished collage.

items.label: A clear scan shows the whole finished collage. What does it add?
items.feedback: A clear whole view can record the finished work. Keep the process records too.

options.label: A promise to finish later.
The final artwork record.

items.label: One section is still loose and the maker wants to finish it. What is honest?
items.feedback: Keep what exists and name the next action. A gap is not filled by ticking a box.

options.label: Name the step left and arrange time.
Mark the whole work finished now.

activitySchema.discussion: Check your real work with an adult or partner. Ask before touching it. Keep both the actual making trail and the final work when it is ready.

activitySchema.heading: Find the maker’s own view
activitySchema.instruction: Sort the example messages. Do they name enjoyment, achievement, or need the maker’s own view?

items.label: “I liked the sound when I folded the paper.”
items.feedback: The maker names something they enjoyed.

items.label: “I made a base that held my shape up.”
items.feedback: The maker names something they achieved.

items.label: “There is a shape on this page.”
items.feedback: This describes an item. Ask what its maker enjoyed or achieved; do not choose that view for them.

items.label: “I enjoyed choosing where the pale patch went.”
items.feedback: The maker names a choice they enjoyed.

activitySchema.discussion: Look across your real A–C work. Choose your own enjoyment or achievement. Try sharing it with one listener and check what they understood.

activitySchema.heading: Keep the message true to its detail
activitySchema.instruction: Label A, B and C in this example artwork. Match each label to the detail that a maker could point to.

items.label: A
items.feedback: A points to the pale patch. Keep that detail if it is what the maker chose to talk about.

items.label: B
items.feedback: B points to the group of short dark marks. They are a visible detail, not proof of the maker’s feelings.

items.label: C
items.feedback: C points to the gap left between the shapes. Ask the maker what the space means to them.

activitySchema.discussion: The example message is “I liked how the pale patch stood out.” Keep those words when you record it. Do not add “all the colours” or “the task was easy”. Then share and record your own true view.
